Ferhat Ay: The Ay lab uses computational and statistical modeling to study how genes are turned on and off (gene regulation) and how this relates to systemic, infectious, and immune-related diseases. A major focus is the 3D structure of the genome: they analyze data from chromatin conformation capture techniques like Hi-C and HiChIP to see how DNA folds inside cells, and how changes in that folding affect development, cell differentiation, and disease. The lab builds its own computational tools, drawing on statistics, graph theory, data mining, and machine learning, to analyze large-scale genomic datasets. They also work on reconstructing the networks that control gene activity, predicting which DNA regions (enhancers) talk to which genes, building models that predict gene expression, and analyzing single-cell data. In short, this is a dry-lab, code-driven group aimed at understanding the genome's 3D organization and regulation, work relevant to development, immunology, and disease research.
Christopher Benedict: The Benedict lab studies how the immune system interacts with cytomegalovirus (CMV), a very common herpesvirus that infects over half of people without usually causing illness. They discovered a new protein complex called GATE that CMV uses to enter cells and to suppress immune defenses from within infected cells, the first new CMV entry complex found in over 20 years, which could inform vaccine development. The lab has also found that CMV infection causes the immune system to dedicate an unusually large share, over 10%, of circulating T cells to fighting it. They are now exploring whether these abundant CMV-specific T cells could be redirected to attack pancreatic cancer instead, potentially creating an off-the-shelf cancer immunotherapy since so many people are already infected with CMV. The work combines virology, immunology, and translational cancer research.
Hilde Cheroutre: The Cheroutre lab studies T lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell, focusing on how the immune system protects the body's interface surfaces (skin, lungs, mouth, and especially the intestine) where the outside world meets the inside of the body. A central question is how the immune system tells the difference between harmful pathogens and harmless things like food or beneficial gut bacteria, and what goes wrong when that distinction fails, since such failures can allow disease-causing agents to invade. The lab has extended this work to immune memory cells that guard against returning pathogens or cancer: certain white blood cells recognize and destroy tumor cells displaying abnormal surface proteins, and some of these cells become long-lived memory cells that react quickly if the tumor returns or spreads. This research is relevant to autoimmune and inflammatory intestinal diseases as well as cancer immunity.
Shane Crotty: The Crotty lab's publicly described focus in this text centers on COVID-19 vaccine research, work that has informed vaccine development efforts worldwide by building on lessons learned from past vaccines and experimental approaches. Beyond this, the provided material is mostly news headlines and awards rather than a detailed description of methods, so specifics on their broader research approach cannot be confidently summarized here. Dr. Crotty has emphasized that vaccine development is a large, collaborative effort requiring extensive time and many people to work out, rather than a quick or simple process. Prospective students interested in this lab would want to reach out directly to learn more about ongoing projects, given the limited methodological detail available in this text.
Einav: The Einav lab tackles a long-standing puzzle in vaccine research: why flu vaccines trigger a strong protective antibody response in some people but almost no response in others, despite decades of study across different ages, species, and vaccine formulations. Rather than running traditional wet-lab experiments, this lab is computational: they use interpretable machine learning algorithms and biophysical models to analyze large amounts of existing immune system data. Their goal is to build a systems-level map of the immune response that can predict how an individual will respond to a given vaccine strain, enabling personalized vaccine selection based on a person's own antibody profile. They also study fundamental tradeoffs in immunity, such as whether a stronger antibody response comes at the cost of being less durable. The lab's stated aim is to discover general, actionable 'laws' of immune system behavior that could guide better vaccine design.
Alba Grifoni: The Grifoni lab studies how the immune system, particularly T cells, responds to viral infections, and specifically which parts of a virus are recognized by these T cells. Their approach combines bioinformatics (computational analysis) with laboratory experiments to study coronaviruses (including SARS-CoV-2 and related viruses), orthopoxviruses (like Mpox and Vaccinia), and other emerging pathogens. Since 2020, the lab has been part of LJI's Coronavirus Taskforce, working with other LJI faculty to show how the immune system fights initial SARS-CoV-2 infection and how T cell memory persists after infection or vaccination, including against variants like Omicron. This research has helped identify additional viral targets for vaccine development. The lab's current work asks how similar these T cell targets are across different coronaviruses, aiming to inform what a vaccine effective against many coronaviruses at once might need to look like.
Hastie: The Hastie lab focuses on antibody discovery and structural biology to fight emerging viral threats. As Director of Antibody Discovery, the lab developed a high-throughput platform that can isolate promising therapeutic and diagnostic antibodies within weeks of a new virus emerging or after immunization, aiming for rapid response to outbreaks. They use structural biology techniques to determine the detailed 3D architecture of viral surface proteins and how these proteins interact with antibodies, revealing weak points ('vulnerabilities') in viruses that are otherwise hard for the immune system to target. One specific project involves characterizing first-in-class antibodies against New World Arenaviruses, a group of rodent-borne viruses that are highly pathogenic and currently have no approved vaccines or treatments. The overall goal is to translate structural insights into new therapeutics and vaccines against dangerous, emerging viral pathogens.
Patrick Hogan: The Hogan lab studies how proteins interact with each other and with DNA at a molecular level to control which genes get turned on inside cells, focusing especially on T cells, the immune system's infection-fighting white blood cells. A major research theme is how calcium entering a T cell triggers the activation of genes needed to fight infections and cancer. This built on Dr. Hogan's earlier work in neurobiology on how sensory neurons use calcium signaling. In a landmark 2006 discovery, the lab identified a protein called ORAI1 as the pore-forming component of the calcium channel in T cells, after finding it mutated in children with severe immune deficiencies. This finding directly links calcium signaling to immune function, and the lab believes targeting this calcium channel could lead to new therapies for transplant rejection and autoimmune disorders.
Mitchell Kronenberg: The provided text for the Kronenberg lab is largely composed of news headlines, awards, and general topic mentions (such as invariant NKT cells and mucosal immunity/IBD project titles) rather than a substantive description of their research questions or methods. It references collaboration with the Cheroutre lab on mucosal immunity and mentions work related to immune cells defending vulnerable organs and T cells implicated in ulcerative colitis, but does not explain the underlying approach in enough detail to responsibly summarize. A student interested in this lab would need to look at the lab's specific project pages or contact lab members directly for a clear picture of current research.
Li: The Li lab studies the molecular interactions that happen at biological membranes, the boundary that separates a cell's inside from its surroundings, since these interactions underlie both how viruses invade cells and how the immune system recognizes threats. For example, viruses use host receptor proteins on the cell surface to gain entry, while immune cells communicate through networks of receptor-ligand interactions, and antibodies or T-cell receptors recognize specific markers on infected or cancerous cells. Dr. Haoyang Li's group uses structural immunology, closely examining these molecular interactions, to understand infection mechanisms, immune signaling, and immune protection at high resolution. Current projects include studying how Old World arenaviruses hijack host receptors to cause infection, designing new Lassa virus vaccine candidates, and investigating molecules that regulate inflammation, with the goal of informing new vaccines and therapies for infections, autoimmune diseases, and cancer.
Samuel Myers: The Myers lab studies how immune cells process the many, sometimes conflicting, signals they receive from their environment, such as balancing the need to fight off pathogens or cancer cells against the need to tolerate harmless gut bacteria and the body's own tissues. These decisions are controlled inside cells by biochemical networks involving protein post-translational modifications (PTMs), small chemical changes rapidly added to and removed from proteins that regulate processes from gene expression to cell death. The lab notes that most PTM research has focused on only a handful of well-known modifications, leaving many others understudied. Using mass spectrometry and quantitative proteomics, combined with genomics, chemical biology, and genetic engineering, the Myers lab maps these global signaling dynamics to understand how different PTMs interact and drive immune cell activation and differentiation, work relevant to autoimmune disease, cardiovascular disease, neurodegeneration, and cancer.
Bjoern Peters: The Peters lab develops computational tools to address fundamental questions in immunology, with a central focus on predicting epitopes: the specific molecular pieces of a pathogen, allergen, or cancer cell that the immune system recognizes and targets. Identifying these epitopes helps researchers develop diagnostics, vaccines, and therapeutics more efficiently. The lab builds machine learning-based prediction tools so that researchers can focus their lab experiments on the molecules most likely to trigger an immune response, rather than testing broadly and inefficiently. This computational approach has been applied to areas including tuberculosis infection and BCG vaccination, whooping cough vaccine immunity, and allergic disease research such as pediatric milk allergy. Overall, this is a bioinformatics-driven lab aiming to make immune target discovery faster and more targeted across a range of infectious and allergic diseases.
Rad: The Rad lab studies B cells, the immune cells that produce antibodies, focusing on how they develop, get activated, and improve their targeting ability over time. Each B cell starts with a unique antibody receptor and remains inactive until it encounters a matching target (antigen), usually in lymph nodes or other peripheral immune tissue. During an immune response, B cells enter specialized structures called germinal centers where they are tested and refined: cells that bind their target well are favored and become stronger responders, while weaker ones are eliminated. The lab studies how this selection process happens, what determines which immune responses are strengthened or lost, and how these choices shape which cells become long-lasting memory B cells or antibody-producing plasma cells. The goal is to better understand how to steer immune responses toward more durable protection, informing future vaccines, diagnostics, and treatments.
Sydney Ramirez: The Ramirez lab studies human immunology with a focus on the upper airway (like the nose and throat) as an immune site, since this area is a common entry point for infections and environmental exposures. They study how immune cells stationed in these tissues contribute to surveillance and protection against pathogens, and how immune memory, the body's ability to 'remember' and quickly respond to a previously encountered threat, is formed and maintained specifically in this mucosal environment. By studying mucosal immunity in both healthy and disease contexts, the lab aims to build a more complete picture of how the body's layered immune defenses work together, particularly relevant to respiratory infections like SARS-CoV-2.
Anjana Rao: The Rao lab studies how immune cells, especially T cells, are controlled at the level of gene expression, combining epigenetics (chemical modifications to DNA that affect gene activity without changing the DNA sequence) with cell signaling research. In 2009, the lab discovered the enzymatic activity of the TET family of proteins, which chemically modify DNA (converting 5-methylcytosine to 5-hydroxymethylcytosine and further products) to regulate gene activity important in development, cell identity, and cancer; loss of TET function is linked to various blood and solid cancers. Separately, in collaboration with the Hogan lab, they showed how calcium entering cells activates a signaling pathway (via calcineurin and the transcription factor NFAT) that turns T cells 'on' for infection-fighting, but can also drive T cells into a weakened, 'exhausted' state seen in cancer and chronic viral infections. Using mouse models of CAR-T cell cancer therapy, the lab has identified specific genes driven by NFAT that contribute to this exhaustion, aiming to inform improved cancer immunotherapies.
Reina: The Reina Lab studies how the immune system protects specific tissues in the body over the long term, focusing on tissue-resident memory T cells (TRM) — immune cells that set up permanent residence in organs like the prostate to guard against disease. Using spatial transcriptomics, a technique that maps the activity of hundreds to thousands of genes directly within intact tissue, the lab is uncovering how TRM cells are organized in tissue, how they adapt metabolically to survive there long-term, and how these adaptations support anti-tumor immunity. The lab also works on immune engineering approaches to boost CD8 T cell function in disease. This matters because non-resectable tumors, chronic infections, and autoimmune complications all depend on whether the right protective immunity is established in the right place at the right time — something not yet well understood.
Erica Ollmann Saphire: The Ollmann Saphire Laboratory studies emerging infectious diseases with the goal of speeding up vaccine and therapeutic development. Their core method is structural biology: determining the detailed 3D shapes of the proteins on the surface of dangerous viruses, including Ebola, Marburg, Bundibugyo, Lassa, rabies, herpesviruses like CMV, and human endogenous retroviruses. These structures reveal exactly how each virus enters human cells, evades the immune system, and could be blocked by drugs or antibodies. The lab has also discovered and characterized some of the first human antibodies with broad protective activity against multiple filoviruses (the Ebola family), as well as novel antibody responses to measles virus. This structural and antibody work provides a direct foundation for designing next-generation vaccines and antibody-based treatments against some of the world's deadliest viral threats.
Schmiedel: The Schmiedel Lab studies why immune cells sometimes malfunction, contributing to autoimmune and inflammatory disease, with a particular focus on how genetics and biological sex shape immune cell function. Their approach centers on generating high-resolution transcriptomic (gene expression) and epigenomic (gene regulation) maps of immune cells from both healthy people and patients. Because genome-wide association studies have linked many common genetic variants to immune disease risk without explaining how those variants actually affect cell behavior, the lab works to connect the dots — identifying which immune cell types and genes are involved. This work is anchored by the NIH-funded DICE database, a resource the lab helped build that catalogs how genetic variation influences immune gene expression. The ultimate goal is to translate these findings into better diagnostics and therapeutic targets for immune-mediated diseases.
Stephen Schoenberger: The Schoenberger Lab studies how the immune system's T cells are triggered and controlled during infection and cancer, with three connected research threads. First, the lab examines how CD4+ 'helper' T cells decide whether to assist or restrain CD8+ 'killer' T cells, depending on the level of inflammation present — insight that could improve vaccine design. Second, the lab builds animal models of cancer immunotherapy, identifying tumor-specific mutations (neoantigens) that can be targeted by vaccines or by transferring engineered T cells into patients, including a discovery about how tumor cells can be converted into neoantigen-carrying cancer stem cells. Third, the lab is part of a clinical program at UC San Diego treating head and neck cancer patients by identifying their tumors' neoantigens and the T cell receptors that recognize them, using next-generation sequencing and single-cell genomics.
Alessandro Sette: The Sette Lab studies how the immune system recognizes disease at a chemical level, focusing on epitopes — the precise molecular structures that immune cells detect and respond to. This knowledge is applied broadly: to cancer, autoimmunity, allergy, and infectious diseases such as pertussis (whooping cough), varicella zoster virus, and Staphylococcus aureus, and in collaborations on vaccines targeting inflammation involved in atherosclerosis. A major, decades-long project led by the lab is the Immune Epitope Database (IEDB), a free, widely used public resource that catalogs epitopes from humans and other species across allergens, infectious diseases, autoantigens, and transplants, and provides prediction tools used by immunology researchers worldwide. By defining exactly what the immune system reacts to, the lab's work informs the design of better vaccines and diagnostic and therapeutic strategies across many diseases.
Sonia Sharma: The Sharma Lab studies how cells detect danger signals and mount immune responses, with a particular focus on type I interferon signaling — a pathway that protects against viruses and tumors but, when overactive, can drive autoimmune disease. The lab investigates how cell-free DNA circulating outside cells is recognized as a threat, including by vascular endothelial cells, which the lab has found mount surprisingly strong innate immune responses to it. Dr. Sharma also directs the Institute's Functional Genomics Center, and her research incorporates human genetics and patient biosamples alongside genome-scale screening approaches. This work aims to clarify how genes contribute to both protective immunity and disease, informing understanding of interferon-driven conditions and potential targets for cancer surveillance and immunotherapy.
Sujan Shresta: The Shresta Lab studies the immunology of major human viral threats, particularly dengue virus, Zika virus, and SARS-CoV-2 (the virus that causes COVID-19). These viruses can cause a wide range of outcomes — dengue can progress from mild fever to life-threatening dengue shock syndrome, Zika can cause serious birth defects and neurological complications, and coronaviruses have repeatedly caused public health emergencies. A key focus is 'cross-reactivity': how prior immune exposure to one virus in a family can shape the immune response to a related virus later. The lab uses mouse models and human cell cultures to study how these viruses interact with the immune system, and validates findings using human samples collected from dengue-endemic countries like Nepal, Thailand, Vietnam, and Japan. This combination of lab models and real-world human data is used to test new vaccines and therapeutics.
Pandurangan Vijayanand: The Vijayanand Lab uses genomics tools to study, diagnose, and work toward treating pulmonary (lung) diseases including asthma, lung cancer, and infectious diseases such as COVID-19. A central puzzle the lab addresses is that many genetic variants have been linked to disease risk, but how those variants actually change gene expression in specific cell types is still largely unknown. To investigate this, the lab has developed techniques to profile the molecular activity of circulating and airway immune cells from patients, using smaller cell samples than were previously required — making it easier to study immune cells directly from patient airways. This genomics-driven approach connects genetic risk factors to the actual behavior of immune cells in lung disease, with the aim of improving diagnosis and treatment for conditions like asthma.
Weiskopf: The Weiskopf Lab studies how human T cells respond to emerging infectious viruses, currently focused on arboviruses (viruses spread by insects such as mosquitoes) — specifically dengue virus, Zika virus, and chikungunya virus, which belong to the Flavivirus and Alphavirus families. The lab previously did extensive work characterizing T cell responses to SARS-CoV-2 following infection and vaccination. A central question driving the research is why infections with these viruses can range from asymptomatic to severe or chronic disease in different people. By studying the interactions between these viruses and the human immune system, the lab aims to understand what drives this variability in symptoms, with the goal of informing better vaccine design and improving diagnosis and treatment strategies for arbovirus diseases.
